title: Loss Functions & Gradient Descent
html:
Training means minimising a loss function — a number that says how wrong the model is. Gradient descent does this by repeatedly stepping the parameters downhill along the negative gradient.

TermMeaning
LossError on one example, e.g. (y − ŷ)²
Cost / objectiveAverage loss over the training set, plus any regularisation penalty — what the optimiser minimises
MetricWhat you care about when evaluating (accuracy, F1, MAE); it need not be differentiable and may differ from the training loss

Common losses

LossFormula (one example)Used byNotes
Squared error (MSE)(y − ŷ)²Linear regression, regression treesPenalises large errors heavily; predicts the conditional mean
Absolute error (MAE)|y − ŷ|Robust regression, quantile modelsLess sensitive to outliers; predicts the conditional median
HuberSquared for |y − ŷ| ≤ δ, linear beyondHuberRegressor, boostingMSE near zero, MAE for outliers
Log-loss (binary cross-entropy)−[y·log p + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)]Logistic regression, boosting, neural netsPunishes confident wrong probabilities without limit
Hingemax(0, 1 − y·f(x)), y ∈ {−1, +1}SVMZero once a point is beyond the margin

Gradient descent

θ ← θ − η · ∇J(θ) η = learning rate, ∇J = gradient of the cost

The gradient points uphill; stepping against it lowers the cost. For linear regression with MSE cost J(θ) = (1/n)·‖Xθ − y‖², the gradient is (2/n)·Xᵀ(Xθ − y):

The learning rate

VariantGradient computed onTrade-off
Batch gradient descentAll n examples each stepExact, smooth; slow for large n
Stochastic (SGD)One example each stepCheap, noisy steps — the noise can escape shallow bumps
Mini-batchA batch of 32–1024 examplesThe practical default: vectorised and reasonably smooth
  • Scale features first — with very different scales the cost surface is a long narrow valley and gradient descent zig-zags.
  • Linear and logistic regression costs are convex: any minimum is the global minimum. Neural-network losses are not (see Deep Learning for momentum, Adam and learning-rate schedules).
  • Stop when the cost stops improving on validation data (early stopping) or after a fixed number of epochs.
What happens if the learning rate is too high or too low?

Too low: tiny steps, very slow convergence, may stall. Too high: steps overshoot the minimum, the cost oscillates or diverges to infinity. Try values on a log scale (0.001, 0.01, 0.1…) and watch the training curve.

Why is log-loss used for classification instead of MSE?

It is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, so minimising it gives maximum-likelihood probabilities. Combined with a sigmoid it is convex in the weights and gives large gradients when the model is confidently wrong; MSE with a sigmoid is non-convex and its gradients vanish on confident mistakes.

Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch gradient descent?

They differ in how many examples are used per update: all of them (accurate but slow), one (fast, noisy), or a small batch (the usual compromise that uses vectorised hardware well).
